document.title: Fast Pseudorandom Correlation Functions from Sparse LPN

candidate.title: The Binary Dual-Distance Bound Is the Worst Case
candidate.subtitle: The union bound computed over F_2 never exceeds the one computed over a larger prime field
candidate.one_line: For the same dimensions, sparsity and failure probability, the dual-distance lower bound the source computes over the binary field is at most the bound its general-field formulae give for any larger prime field.
candidate.informal: Every concrete parameter set for a sparse-LPN-based construction rests on the dual distance of the random sparse code matrix, and nobody computes it -- what is computed is a union-bound lower bound on it, tractably only over the binary field. Constructions over a larger field use the binary number anyway, on the belief that a larger field can only help, since cancellation then needs matching supports and matching values. This conjecture is that belief made precise: the binary bound never exceeds the large-field bound at the same parameters. Both sides are explicit finite sums, so a single parameter triple would refute it.
candidate.status_note: Open, and asserted rather than asked: the source writes that it expects the binary bound to lower-bound the bound over larger fields, gives an intuition, records that all previous work assumes as much, and proves nothing. No counterexample is known and no proof is known.
candidate.progress_note: The source proves neither direction and provides general-field formulae it does not evaluate, because the cost is at least cubic in the dimension. The intuition it offers -- cancellation over a larger field needs opposite values, not just colliding supports -- addresses only one of the two competing effects; the other, that a larger field multiplies the number of candidate kernel vectors of each support by (p-1)^w, appears in the general-field summand and is not discussed.

quotes.text: However, we expect the bound obtained through our analysis over F2 to provide a lower bound on that over larger fields.
All previous works assume that the bound does not degrade as the field size grows and a common heuristic is, therefore, to use the bounds from the analysis over F2
Note that the complexity of the computation is at least cubic in the LPN dimension n and quickly becomes infeasible for the large dimensions that we are interested in.
Intuitively, as the field grows, canceling rows gets harder; it no longer suffices for balls to land in the same bins but they must have opposite values.

Our analysis above exploits properties of F2 (e.g., cancellations are more likely compared to a general field and only even-weight vectors matter). This allows us to run our implementation to run up to large values of n (see below), but makes it incompatible with general fields Fp.
In Section 4.3 we gave explicit formulae to compute the dual distance of regular random codes
D = 0 indicates that we can only guarantee a trivial bound

candidate.why_interesting: It is the load-bearing heuristic under every concrete sparse-LPN parameter set over a large field, including the source's own and those of the zero-knowledge systems it cites. If it holds, those parameter sets are conservative; if it fails at parameters anyone uses, they overstate the linear-test security level they target.
candidate.why_clean: Both sides are explicit finite sums of rationals defined in the source, so the statement is decidable at any single parameter triple and refutable by one counterexample.
candidate.risks: The two bounds are computed for different code ensembles -- the F_2 side for the regular ensemble, the general-field side for the sparse ensemble -- which is a feature of the source's sentence and not of this transcription, and is the first thing to check. A structural consequence is that the F_2 sum runs over even weights only while the general-field sum runs over all weights. The source's extension remark (replace p_{w,0}^k by p_{w.k,0}) gives a same-ensemble variant of the claim that is arguably the more natural one, and is deliberately not what is stated.
candidate.formal_statement_latex: For every prime $p > 2$, every $\rho > 0$, and all integers $3 \le k \le n$ with $k \mid n$ and $m \ge 1$, $D_{2}(k, m, n, \rho) \le D_{p}(k, m, n, \rho)$, where $D_{2}$ is the bound of the source's Section 4.3 (over $\F_{2}$, regular ensemble) and $D_{p}$ that of its Section 4.5 (over $\F_{p}$, sparse ensemble), each taken to be $0$ when no $d$ satisfies its constraint.

verify.reason: The claim is printed as a belief the source holds and does not prove ('we expect ... to provide a lower bound'), it is load-bearing for the source's own large-field parameter selection, and nothing later in the paper proves it -- Section 4.5 supplies formulae and then says evaluating them is infeasible at the dimensions of interest. The correction that mattered: the two bounds the source's sentence compares are computed for different code ensembles, which the first draft did not say.

checks.name: existence
checks.finding: Printed on p. 26 in the paragraph 'Analysis Over a General Field', confirmed by rendering the page at 150 dpi.

checks.name: openness
checks.finding: Not proved anywhere: the numbered results are Theorem 1, Lemmas 2-6 and Claims 1-2, none about field size, and Section 4.5's closing paragraph says the general-field computation is at least cubic in n and infeasible at the dimensions of interest. The source's phrasing is 'we expect', and it records that previous work merely assumes it.

checks.name: strength
checks.finding: The source's sentence compares its F_2 analysis (Section 4.3, RegularCodeGen) with the general-field analysis (Section 4.5, SparseCodeGen), so the two sides are different ensembles as well as different fields. The first draft stated the inequality without recording this. Corrected by naming both ensembles in the definitions and adding the remark; the same-ensemble variant is explicitly not what is stated.

checks.name: quantifiers-and-parameters
checks.finding: Universally quantified over p, rho, k, n, m, as the source's unrestricted sentence implies; the D = 0 convention for a trivial bound is the source's own, from the Table 2 caption on p. 28.

checks.name: attribution
checks.finding: The expectation is the source's own ('we expect'). The practice of using the binary bound over larger fields is attributed to previous work, as the source attributes it, to ADINZ17 and BCGI18.

checks.name: definitions
checks.finding: Both formulae were transcribed from rendered images of pp. 26 and 30 rather than from the text layer, which drops the fraction in N := n/k and prints it as 'nk'. SparseCodeGen and RegularCodeGen are the source's Definitions 3 and 4, p. 11.

checks.name: fabrication
checks.finding: The remark about the (p-1)^w factor is labelled as an observation about the source's own printed summand, not as a claim of the source's. No claim is attributed to the source that it does not make.

checks.name: self-containment
checks.finding: The two probabilities q_w and pi^(p)_w are defined probabilistically on the page, so both bounds are fully determined without the source's recursions.

corrections.problem: The two bounds were stated without recording that D_2 is computed for the regular ensemble and D_p for the sparse ensemble.
corrections.corrected: Name the ensemble in each definition and add the remark on the mismatch and on the even-weight-only structure of the F_2 sum.

corrections.problem: No convention for the case where the constraint fails at w = 1, where the max is over an empty set.
corrections.corrected: Set the value to 0 in that case, following the source's own Table 2 caption.

corrections.problem: N := n/k was first read off the text layer, which renders it 'nk'.
corrections.corrected: Transcribe from the rendered page: N := n/k, the length of one block of a regular row.

rejected_in_this_paper.what: The conjecture that a high dual distance is all that is needed for a sparse LPN instance to be as secure as standard LPN (Section 4.2, p. 23).
rejected_in_this_paper.why: Not the source's own conjecture -- it attributes it to ADINZ17 and BCM25 -- and the source says it is not formalizable as stated: 'Note that the conjecture is not fully formal: there are known counter-examples (typically, Reed-Solomon codes)'. A page would have to invent the formalization the literature has not settled.

rejected_in_this_paper.what: The binary-SVP-style assumption that low-weight kernel vectors are hard to find even when they exist (Section 4.2, p. 24).
rejected_in_this_paper.why: The source calls it a 'very reasonable assumption' that was 'explicitly required and studied in multiple works', i.e. an assumption the parameter selection makes, not an open problem this paper poses. prompts/harvest.md rejects security assumptions dressed as conjectures by name.

rejected_in_this_paper.what: Whether the sparse-product noise distribution used for the stateless variant affects security (Section 1.5, p. 10).
rejected_in_this_paper.why: The source says only that it 'does not appear to have any impact on security' while cautioning that a new construction warrants care. That is a hedge about its own optimization, with no proposition attached and no claim that anything is open.

rejected_in_this_paper.what: Extending the concrete dual-distance computation to general fields at the dimensions the construction uses (Section 4.5, p. 32).
rejected_in_this_paper.why: An engineering and algorithmic-cost problem -- the formulae exist and are at least cubic in n -- rather than a mathematical claim to prove or refute. It is recorded as the obstruction on the page for the field-size conjecture instead.
